title: Germany: Oktoberfest beer prices rise, outpacing inflation
summary: Oktoberfest's traditional beer mug, the Mass, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) at this year's festival in Munich.

image.caption: Between 6 million and 7 million visitors are expected in Munich this year [FILE: September 2023]Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: The price of a liter of beer at Munich's Oktoberfest has risen fivefold since 1985, far outpacing overall inflation in Germany, according to an analysis by UniCredit's chief economist in Germany, Andreas Rees.

A Mass, the traditional 1-liter (2.1-pint) serving at Oktoberfest, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) this year. In 1985, it cost about 6.25 Deutschmarks, equivalent to €3.20 after conversion at the fixed euro exchange rate.
The figures were analyzed by UniCredit economist Andreas Rees ahead of the opening of the world's largest beer festival on Saturday.
Beer prices at Oktoberfest have increased by around 400% since 1985, according to Rees, using data from Munich's statistical office.
Consumer prices across Germany, by comparison, have risen by around 120% over the same period.
This year's increase is considerably more modest. The average price of a Mass is up 2.4% from last year, below Germany's expected overall inflation rate of close to 3%.
"Beer prices at the Oktoberfest depend on a peculiar cocktail of harvests, energy prices, wages, tent costs, security and the willingness of millions of visitors to spend generously," Rees said.
Although the trend has been one of sharply rising prices, this year's Mass saw a price of 2.4% compared to 2025, the smallest increase in two decades.
Rees explained that ingredient prices could be playing a role, as hops have become cheaper while malting-barley prices have stabilized.
Oktoberfest is the largest folk festival in the world. Locals and tourists alike wear the traditional Bavarian lederhosen and dirndl dresses on the festival grounds.

The festival dates back to 1810, and it takes place at the Wiesn, a the local dialect abbreviation for Theresienwiese, the fairgrounds in Munich named in honor of Crown Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen.
This Saturday, Munich will celebrate the 191st Oktoberfest, expecting somewhere between 6 and 7 million visitors.
The party begins when the city's mayor opens the first barrel in a ceremony officially marking the opening of the festival.
